name: Thebes
info: Thebes was the leading polis of the Boeotian League in central Greece, remembered for Epaminondas's victory over Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC and its destruction by Alexander the Great in 335 BC.

facts.capital: Thebes, with its citadel, the Cadmea
facts.founder: not known; Greek tradition named Cadmus, a Phoenician prince from Tyre
facts.predecessor: The Mycenaean settlement of the Bronze Age at the Cadmea
facts.successor: Roman rule after the Achaean War of 146 BC; the Province of Achaia from 27 BC

t: Thebes was the largest and leading polis of the Boeotian League and was often called "Seven-Gated Thebes".
The Theban army trained and led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas defeated the Spartans at Leuctra in 371 BC, beginning a short Theban hegemony.
After a revolt in 335 BC Alexander the Great destroyed the city and sold the Thebans into slavery; Cassander re-established it in 315 BC.
dyk: When Alexander destroyed Thebes in 335 BC, tradition holds that he spared only the temples and the house of the poet Pindar, along with priests, the pro-Macedonian party and Pindar's descendants.
ev: During the Persian invasion of Greece the governing aristocracy of Thebes joined Xerxes I and fought for him at the Battle of Plataea
At the head of the Boeotian levy the Thebans defeated an Athenian army at the Battle of Delium
A Spartan force seized the Cadmea by a coup de main; it was expelled three years later and a democratic constitution set up
Theban forces under Epaminondas defeated the Spartans at the Battle of Leuctra
Epaminondas died at the Battle of Mantinea and Thebes sank back to a secondary power
Philip II of Macedon defeated Thebes and Athens at the Battle of Chaeronea
Alexander the Great destroyed Thebes after its revolt and sold its people into slavery
Cassander re-established Thebes with labour and money from other Greek cities

sections.foundation:
Excavations in and around Thebes have revealed a Mycenaean settlement, cist graves holding weapons and ivory, and clay tablets written in the Linear B script, which name the place as te-qa-i, "at Thebes". It was one of the first Greek communities drawn together within a fortified city, and it owed its importance to its military strength. In the late Bronze Age it drew resources from Lamos near Mount Helicon and from Karystos and Amarynthos on Euboia.

The central area, the Cadmea, shows signs of destruction towards the end of the Mycenaean era, and much of the site was abandoned. The Homeric Hypothebai, or "sub-Thebes", may have been the seed of the Archaic and Classical polity when the city was reestablished. Greek legend made Cadmus, a Phoenician prince from Tyre, the founder of the citadel and the teacher of the Phoenician alphabet, and set at Thebes the stories of Semele and Dionysus, Amphion's seven-gated wall, Oedipus and the Seven against Thebes, and the birth of Heracles. The Theban nobility bore the name Spartoi, "Sown Men", explained by the myth of Cadmus.
sections.socioeconomy:
Thebes stands in a plain of Boeotia between Lake Yliki, the ancient Hylica, to the north and the Cithaeron mountains, which divide Boeotia from Attica, to the south, about 50 km northwest of Athens. The city was the largest in Boeotia and the centre of the region, and its rule over the smaller Boeotian towns was the constant aim of its policy and the constant cause of its quarrels with Athens and Sparta.

The saved sources say little of the classical city's economy beyond its standing as the chief market and fortress of the plain. Its society was led for long periods by a traditional oligarchy, the governing aristocracy that took the Persian side in 480 BC, until a democratic constitution replaced it after 379 BC. Thebes produced the poet Pindar, the painters Aristides and Nicomachus and the Cynic philosopher Crates. It was famous in antiquity for the practice of pedagogic pederasty, for which some ancients found an origin in the myth of Laius and Chrysippus. Thebes was revered as the most ancient of Greek cities, with a history of over 1,000 years.
sections.military:
Thebes rose on its army. In 506 BC the Thebans repelled an inroad into Attica; in 480 BC they sent 400 men to Thermopylae, who were defeated alongside the Spartans, and then fought for Xerxes I at the Battle of Plataea in 479 BC. The Cadmea held out as a base when the Athenians occupied the rest of Boeotia from 457 to 447 BC. In the Peloponnesian War the Thebans besieged Plataea in 431 BC, destroyed it after its capture in 427 BC and, in 424 BC, defeated an Athenian army at the Battle of Delium.

They stood their ground against the Spartans at the Battle of Haliartus in 395 BC and the Battle of Coronea in 394 BC. Trained and led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas, with the Sacred Band of Thebes, the Theban army won at Leuctra in 371 BC, then carried its arms into the Peloponnesus, freeing many helots, and sent expeditions to Thessaly and Macedon. Epaminondas fell at Mantinea in 362 BC. In the Third Sacred War against Phocis (356–346 BC) Thebes lost its predominance, and its contingent lost the decisive Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC.
sections.governance:
Thebes headed the Boeotian League, and its presidency of the league was the measure of its power: the victorious Greeks took it away after 479 BC, Sparta restored Thebes as the dominant power in Boeotia in 457 BC, and the general settlement of 387 BC, which declared the autonomy of all Greek towns, withdrew the other Boeotians from its control again. Thebes was also a member of the Delphic amphictyony, from which Sparta tried and failed to expel it after the Persian Wars.

For much of its history the city was governed by a traditional oligarchy. In 379 BC, when the Spartan garrison that had held the Cadmea since 382 BC was expelled, a democratic constitution was set up in its place. The leading men of that democracy, Epaminondas and Pelopidas, were generals and statesmen at once. After Chaeronea Philip II deprived Thebes of its dominion over Boeotia, and the destruction of 335 BC ended the city's independent government until Cassander restored it. In its last free decades it changed masters often, recovering its autonomy from Demetrius Poliorcetes in 287 BC and allying itself with Lysimachus and the Aetolian League.
sections.impact:
Thebes changed the balance of the Greek world more than once. Its aristocracy's support for Xerxes I in 480–479 BC marked it for generations, and its hostility to Athens over Plataea made it a firm ally of Sparta in the Peloponnesian War. After Athens fell, Thebes turned on Sparta, and the victory at Leuctra in 371 BC permanently crippled Spartan power, in part by freeing many of the helots on whom the Spartan economy rested. Its army was regulating the affairs of Thessaly and Macedon in the following years.

Philip II of Macedon had been raised in Thebes as a hostage and had learnt much of the art of war from Pelopidas, so the city also shaped the power that overthrew it. Its destruction in 335 BC cowed Athens into submission. Ancient writers treated the destruction as excessive, and Plutarch reports that Alexander later tried to make amends to any Theban he met. Beyond politics, Thebes gave Greek literature the great Theban cycle of legend, the stories of Cadmus, Oedipus, the Seven against Thebes and the Epigoni, which rival the myths of Troy in their influence on classical writing.
sections.decline:
The Theban hegemony was short-lived: the states it protected would not accept its control for long, and Athens worked to prevent a Theban empire. With the death of Epaminondas at Mantinea in 362 BC Thebes became a secondary power. By asking Philip II to crush the Phocians it brought Macedonian power close to its borders, and in 338 BC, persuaded by Demosthenes, it joined Athens and lost at Chaeronea. When it revolted against Alexander in 335 BC while he campaigned in the north, he and his Greek allies destroyed the city, divided its land among the other Boeotian cities and sold its people into slavery.

Cassander re-established Thebes in 315 BC; the Athenians rebuilt much of its wall, and help came from Megalopolis, Messene, Sicily and Italy. The city never regained its former standing. Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged it in 293 BC and again after a revolt in 292 BC, taking it a second time. After the dissolution of the Boeotian League following the Achaean War of 146 BC, Thebes came under Roman rule, and in 27 BC it was included in the Province of Achaia. The city itself lived on, later the capital of the Byzantine Theme of Hellas and a great centre of silk weaving.

summary: Thebes was the chief city of Boeotia and head of the Boeotian League. It sided with Persia in 480 BC, fought beside Sparta and then against it, and under Epaminondas won the hegemony of Greece at Leuctra in 371 BC. Defeated by Macedon at Chaeronea and destroyed by Alexander in 335 BC, it was rebuilt by Cassander but never recovered, and came under Rome in 146 BC.

pointDescs.-900: The register's starting date for the polity; the saved article dates no event to it, saying only that the Archaic city was reestablished after the Mycenaean site was largely abandoned.
pointDescs.-506: The Thebans, already in conflict with Athens over Plataea, repelled an inroad into Attica.
pointDescs.-479: After its aristocracy fought for Xerxes I at the Battle of Plataea, the victorious Greeks deprived Thebes of the presidency of the Boeotian League.
pointDescs.-457: Sparta, needing a counterweight to Athens, reinstated Thebes as the dominant power in Boeotia.
pointDescs.-424: Leading the Boeotian levy, the Thebans defeated an invading Athenian force at the Battle of Delium.
pointDescs.-387: The general settlement declaring the autonomy of all Greek towns withdrew the other Boeotians from Theban control.
pointDescs.-382: A Spartan force occupied the Cadmea by a treacherous coup de main.
pointDescs.-371: The Theban army under Epaminondas defeated the Spartans at Leuctra and went on to cripple Spartan power in the Peloponnese.
pointDescs.-362: Epaminondas died at the Battle of Mantinea and Thebes sank again to a secondary power.
pointDescs.-338: The Theban contingent lost the decisive Battle of Chaeronea to Philip II, who took away its dominion over Boeotia.
pointDescs.-335: After a failed revolt Alexander the Great destroyed the city and sold the Thebans into slavery.
pointDescs.-315: Cassander re-established Thebes, with other Greek cities providing labour and money.
pointDescs.-292: Demetrius Poliorcetes, who had besieged Thebes in 293 BC, took it again after a revolt.
pointDescs.-287: Thebes recovered its autonomy from Demetrius and allied itself with Lysimachus and the Aetolian League.
pointDescs.-146: After the Achaean War the Boeotian League was dissolved and Thebes came under Roman rule.

notes: The register's start year -900 is not dated by the article; the first point is placed there only because the brief requires it.
The article gives no reference list (only Pleiades in external links), so references are empty.
The socioeconomy section is thin: the article says almost nothing of the classical city's economy; I described its setting, society and notable people instead.
